scoring: priority = impact (1-5) x confidence (0-1) / effort (1-5); severity classes are ranked before score. Estimates are judgements, not measurements.

items.title: Rule-based turn/task classification has no labelled evaluation set
items.problem: Classifier accuracy is only checked by a handful of unit cases; no way to measure whether a rule change helps or hurts overall.
items.benefit: Measurable accuracy; regressions visible when rules change.
acceptance: ≥80 labelled synthetic examples across relations and categories
Script reports accuracy per class
Baseline recorded; test enforces a floor
items.evidence_of_completion: Labelled fixture (90 cases) + held-out set (45). Baseline tuned: relations 95%, ambiguity 100%, categories 93%. After targeted rule fixes: 100/100/100. Held-out (measured once, not tuned): relations 89%, ambiguity 100%, categories 74%; all held-out category misses fall back to 'general'. Floors enforced in src/test/intentEval.test.ts.

items.title: Category recall on unseen phrasings is 74%
items.problem: Held-out misses: coin change, segfault, off-by-one, regex explanation, 'timeline at scale', SQL phrased without SQL keywords. All fall back to 'general' (safe but loses the specialised structure).
items.benefit: More answers get the right structure.
acceptance: Write a NEW held-out set before tuning
Tune on current holdout folded into the tuned set
New holdout category accuracy > 74% with no tuned-set regression
items.notes: Consider a provider-backed classifier only for low-confidence cases if rules plateau; that costs a model call and latency, so measure first.
items.evidence_of_completion: Protocol followed: holdout #1 folded into tuned set; holdout #2 written BEFORE tuning. Tuned set: relations 96%, ambiguity 100%, categories 99%. Holdout #2 (untouched): relations 78%, categories 42%. Rule fixes on tuned misses did not move holdout #2 at all (10/24 before and after) — keyword rules do not generalise to new phrasings. Mitigation shipped: the 'general' fallback strategy now tells the model to choose the task's structure itself, so a miss degrades to a reasonable answer instead of a generic one. Floors set at measured holdout values.
items.lesson: Stop tuning keyword rules; each rule fixes only the phrasing it was written for.

items.title: Format the remaining legacy files in one dedicated commit
items.problem: 70 files predate Prettier. Changed-files formatting avoids churn but leaves the tree inconsistent.
items.benefit: Consistent style; CI could check everything.
acceptance: One formatting-only commit; tests pass; then CI runs format:all
items.verification: npm run format:all; npm run check
items.notes: Do it on its own so the diff is reviewable as pure formatting; ask before merging if other branches are in flight.

items.title: Measure whether classification misses hurt answers before replacing the rules
items.problem: Category recall on unseen phrasing is 42%, but misses fall back to 'general', which now asks the model to pick the structure. Unknown: does a miss actually produce a worse answer? If not, a model-based classifier would add cost and latency for nothing.
items.benefit: Decide with data whether a classifier call is worth its latency/cost.
acceptance: With an API key: run the same 24 holdout prompts with forced-correct vs actual category; grade answer structure with a rubric (not an LLM judge alone); record cost/latency of an extra classifier call

No tuned-set regression; re-measure on a NEW holdout
items.notes: Holdout #2 is now contaminated for this case once fixed; write holdout #3 first. 2026-10-23: added leak/freeze/hang to the debugging rule ('slow' rejected: it mislabelled a React performance question). Holdout #3 (written first): categories 11/18 -> 13/18, wrong templates 5 -> 3. Holdout #2 10/24 -> 12/24; tuned set unchanged. Remaining wrong templates: memory-growth phrasing without 'leak', and 'throw <code>'. Holdout #3 is now seen; write #4 before further tuning.
